extracted.intended_audience: architects, students of architecture, artists, patrons, and art critics
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance on selecting, teaching, and applying an architectural style (especially Gothic/Classical choices), plus rules for ornamentation, materials, and the social/political role of architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin teaching with strict, imitable rules
rubrics_metrics.description: When teaching architecture (as with teaching writing or Latin), pupils must first be made to copy absolutely and require absolute accuracy in the formation of forms; an authority is required for every expression at first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Force precise imitation of accepted modes until mastery; prevent variations until the student has command of the 'grammar' of the style. Analogy: teach children to write by copyism; allow license only after mastery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study canonical examples and laws of proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine which buildings are to be considered authoritative (e.g., 'Augustan' examples); their modes of construction and laws of proportion are to be studied with penetrating care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify and measure accepted examples; use them as grammatical authorities before attempting variations. Example authorities for decoration: North door of Rouen and St. Urbain at Troyes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalogue forms and decorations as a grammatical system
rubrics_metrics.description: Class the different forms and uses of decorations and catalogue them like a grammarian classes the powers of prepositions; begin work under this absolute, irrefutable authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a systematic taxonomy of decorative elements and their proper applications; initially admit only minute alterations (e.g., slight changes in cavetto depth or fillet breadth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit individual license only after mastery and within limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A license to change or add to received forms may be permitted only after one can 'speak this dead language naturally'; individual authority must still operate within certain limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow creative variation primarily in decoration and only when the practitioner can apply the style naturally and usefully; guard against wholesale departures until a national competence exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a unanimous national style for practicality
rubrics_metrics.description: It is our duty to desire an unanimous style of some kind, and such comprehension and practice of it as would enable adaptation to every kind of building (domestic, civil, ecclesiastical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specific chosen style is less important than unanimity and capacity to adapt its features to different building types; aim for national consistency to improve craftsmanship and economies of scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose style with regard to fiscal adaptability and public sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: Style choice should consider the facility of adaptation to general purposes and the sympathy with which a style would be popularly regarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate styles not only for artistic merit but for economic suitability, ease of use across common building types, and the likely popular reception; avoid choices that are impractical or unpopular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer historically suitable Gothic (early English decorated)
rubrics_metrics.description: The safest choice for modern uses in general is likely the English earliest decorated Gothic, possibly enriched by selected decorative elements from French decorated Gothic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid wholesale adoption of Greek or other inappropriate classical forms for modern everyday uses; where foreign elements are used, accept only well-known examples as limiting authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude infantile, barbarous, or ungovernable styles
rubrics_metrics.description: Styles that are essentially infantine or barbarous (e.g., Norman, Lombard Romanesque) or whose grammatical laws cannot be limited (e.g., French Flamboyant) should be precluded from adoption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not choose styles that are either crude in origin or too loose to be systematized; beware of impotent degradations like Tudor or overly-decorative, unregulated forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select styles whose grammatical laws are limitable and arrangable
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer styles where the 'grammatical laws' can be limited and arranged so that they can be taught, understood, and consistently applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A style that cannot be reduced to teachable, repeatable rules will hinder uniform practice and education; this is a key criterion in choosing among candidate styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exemplary works as final limiting authorities for decoration
rubrics_metrics.description: For matters of decoration, accept certain well-known examples as final and limiting authorities (the author cites specific French examples to follow).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When borrowing decorative motifs, use a small set of acknowledged exemplary works to determine correct application and limits; this prevents arbitrary eclecticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic restraint yields technical, moral, and social benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Concentration on one adopted style will enlarge the architect's understanding, secure practical knowledge, stimulate disciplined imagination, and produce broader social benefits (economy, fellowship, reduced rivalry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize the wider consequences of unified practice: economy of materials and labor, improved domestic comfort, harmonious streets, and positive civic morale; treat stylistic policy as public policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture as meaningful occupation for national good
rubrics_metrics.description: Public expenditure should favor building works that provide technical/intellectual employment (building houses and churches) rather than pointless labor (e.g., moving earth for its own sake).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer projects that cultivate mechanical ingenuity, artistic development, and mental interest among workers; architecture should supply occupation that improves and elevates workers' lives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer crafts that develop skill and intellect over trivial tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Work that cultivates dexterity, patience, and ingenuity (e.g., carving stone, building churches) is morally and socially preferable to occupations that 'burn out' talents (e.g., facet-cutting for jewelry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize forms of labor that allow the worker's qualities to develop; such work provides mental pleasure and communal benefit, and is a philanthropic ideal for employment policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trefoil and foliation as essential Gothic elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The trefoil (and foliation) is the most distinctive feature of the perfect Gothic style — 'the very soul of it' — and the loveliest Gothic is formed on simple and bold tracings of it between blank lancet and overcharged cinquefoiled arches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insist on trefoil forms and bold simple tracings in Gothic work; pay intimate attention to foliation relationships when designing tracery and ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Window and tracery construction should follow simple geometric methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of constructive geometry (e.g., quatrefoil construction by four circles in contact within a large circle, tangents and inner circle truncating cusps) demonstrate that many traceries are exceedingly simple in construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear geometric constructions for traceries and quatrefoils rather than arbitrary ornament; measure and analyze existing successful examples to derive construction rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using iron as a primary constructive material
rubrics_metrics.description: Iron should not be admitted as a constructive material because it is corruptible by rust and fallacious in strength (unequal veins in the metal), though in some cases binding with iron may be preferable to worse structural expedients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise caution in structural reliance on iron; prefer traditional structural solutions unless iron is used temporarily or as binding where it is demonstrably safer than an alternative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Column decoration: avoid painted vertical lines as a rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Never paint a column with vertical lines; however, patterns that give opposing lines (e.g., diamonds or sturgeon-bone patterns) may be applied parallel to the main structure or spirally as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply column ornament so that the pattern harmonizes with the column's form — vertical painting that creates false perception is discouraged, but certain repeat patterns can be used effectively in vertical or spiral arrangements.
